I ran an accidental experiment the entire first month of 2026:

I stopped my usual cadence of commenting on other people’s posts. Not intentionally—I’ve just been working nonstop and haven’t had time for anything else, LinkedIn engagement included.

What used to be 200+ comments per week plummeted to about 30. And most of those were responses to comments on my own posts.

And there were pretty clear consequences as a result: 

📉 My reach dropped to about 10% of its normal level. One TENTH of the impressions I usually get.

(Yes, that's even including the "new" new normal of everyone seeing decreased reach on LinkedIn.)

Turns out showing up and engaging in comments actually IS the best growth strategy on LinkedIn. Pair the commenting with a regular cadence of thoughtful posts and watch your audience and reach grow. This is how you help your community find you and build a meaningful following.

I’m feeling the consequences of *only* posting over the past few weeks without the engagement piece. And it’s more than confirmed what I’ve been saying for months: you can’t be a LinkedIn creator without putting in the work to engage with others.

Post and ghost is dead.

I’ve never really used LinkedIn to talk about myself.
Most of my energy has gone into the work.

I’m 39, almost 40.
An Indian woman. Single. Unmarried.
And professionally where I am today because of choices that weren’t always easy or obvious.

For a long time, I stayed quiet about that.
Partly because I didn’t want my personal life to define my professional one.
Partly because pushing back, especially on subtle things, often feels inefficient.

But silence has a cost.

What shapes careers isn’t usually extreme views.
It’s everyday assumptions.
The quiet biases we adjust ourselves around.

I’ve made sacrifices to get here, and I’m proud of what I’ve built.
At the same time, I don’t believe sacrifice should be the default price women pay for ambition.

I benefit every day from women before me who questioned norms, sometimes quietly, sometimes visibly.
Because they did, I have options they didn’t.

So this is me choosing to acknowledge that.

If you’re a woman early in your career who’s holding back because it feels easier, I see you.
And if you’re a leader shaping teams and decisions, it’s worth noticing whose voices come easily in the room, and whose don’t.

I’m here because someone made it possible for me to be.
I’d like to pass that forward.

HR: What was your previous monthly salary?
Candidate: ₹28,000.

HR: We can offer ₹30,000. It's a reasonable increase.

Candidate: Considering my skills, certifications, and experience, I was expecting ₹40,000.

HR: Salary expectations need to be realistic. You'll gain significant learning opportunities here.
Candidate (hesitantly): Okay... I'll accept the offer.

Two months later...

The candidate was assigned work and additional responsibilities. Performance was consistently strong, and deadlines were always met. However, there was no recognition, and the workload doubled.

Subsequently, a new offer was received – ₹45,000 per month. The candidate resigned.

Manager: "You should have informed us; we could have done something..."
The reality was:

When it mattered, nothing was done.

Lesson: Do not disregard an individual's stated worth.

Offering a lower salary with the promise of "learning opportunities" is a sophisticated form of a toxic work environment.

Talent is retained through respect, not merely time.

The best thing you can do for your job search this weekend? Nothing.


If you're in a job search right now, give yourself permission to log off this weekend.

I've been on both sides of the hiring desk over the last 20 years. One thing I know for sure is that job search fatigue shows up in interviews. Even with the right experience, exhaustion comes through. It costs opportunities.

I've fallen into this trap before. The compulsion to check LinkedIn one more time. The guilt when you're not "doing something." But the search runs 24/7 if you don't set boundaries.

I am doing this right now. Making time for life outside the search and giving myself time to recharge and refocus. It sounds counterintuitive, but it's necessary. When I land that interview, I need to show up as my best self, not the burned-out version running on fumes.

Connecting authentically with recruiters and hiring managers is your path to real opportunities. But authenticity requires energy. Showing up sharp requires rest.

This is an incredibly challenging time to be searching. The pressure is intense. But treating your search like a full-time job means you also get to clock out.

This weekend? Log off. Disconnect. Rest. You'll need that energy next week.

Hot take: Your friend group is killing your growth.

When I was in college and joined Computer Science, I knew nothing about coding or what it was, and even though I had tons of mentorship opportunities at my college ( seniors, alumni, etc), I chose to do it all alone.

Prep alone.
Study alone. 
Apply alone.

Because what happens when you have people around you is that you start comparing your journey with theirs, and sometimes that might motivate you or limit you. 

For me personally, not having a friend group to study along with , let me explore new heights, now I could compare myself with anyone around the world, I could look at their LinkedIn profile and see what all they have done, and do the same. 

Instead if I had limited myself to the people around me, or my college, or my seniors, I would have only achieved what they did ( at max!)

So, go take a look at people who are further away from you and have absolutely no idea that you're even take inspiration from them. 

That's how I keep doing more, keep wanting more. Because if you look further away, there's always someone ahead of you and that's a reason to strive to be better, not out of jealousy, or competition, but just for the sake of your own self. 

Because you deserve to show yourself how much you can achieve.

When I was at ClickUp, I had the privilege of leading the company’s first-ever Super Bowl ad, a project that we approached differently on purpose. Instead of outsourcing, we took the risk of creating it entirely in-house with our incredibly talented internal team. What we built wasn’t just an ad... it was a statement about who we were and how we work.

LinkedIn interviewed me a few weeks ago about the process and what I think goes into creating a great ad:  

1. Consider, are you creating something worthy of real discourse?
2. Make it relevant beyond the walls of your office.
3. Prioritize the audience over internal approval.
4. Start with a foundation people can relate to.
5. Look for what your industry hasn’t done yet.
6. Be okay with negative opinions.
7. Invite the right amount of people into the process — not everyone.
8. Take the risk, even when it’s uncomfortable.

it’s just buried under time.

The image was foggy.
But it wasn’t broken.
And the design wasn’t the problem.

It just needed cleaning, realignment, and care.

Years ago, in one of my companies, sales started to drop.
Everyone’s first reaction was:
“We need a new model.”
“A new system.”
“A complete change.”

Before replacing anything, I stopped and looked closely.

The product still had value.
The sales process had worked for years.
The real issue was simple:
Follow-ups were weaker.
Customer attention had faded.
Small disciplines we once respected were neglected.

We didn’t replace the business.
We restored it.

We cleaned the process.
Realigned the team.
Paid attention again.

Sales came back.
So did momentum.
Without extra cost.

That taught me this lesson:
Most businesses don’t fail because they’re old.
They fail because they stop being maintained.

Sometimes the solution isn’t a new lens —
it’s a clearer one.

I have finally worked up the nerve to say (post on LinkedIn) the quiet part aloud: cybersecurity events are drowning in panel sessions, and it is killing the value of these conferences.

Panels have become the default agenda item, not because they are effective, but because they are easy. Easy for speakers (minimal prep). Easy for coordinators (more names on the flyer). Easy for the audience (little consequence if skipped).

Let’s be honest. Most panels deliver the same high-level talking points with surface‑level insights. Next time, count the number of times you hear a panel member say: “I agree.” Too many panelists seem like they are winging it, avoiding disagreement, and staying miles away from anything that might generate tension, originality, or depth.

Moderators either dominate the conversation or lose control of it completely.

The result? We get shallow conversations with no actionable insights. There is no memorable story, nor little display of expertise.

That is why I have stopped attending most cybersecurity events. If I walk away learning nothing new, what is the point? Are attention spans so fragile that audiences can only manage 90‑second sound bites?

I don’t buy that. We need to bring back real presentations that:
   -  Tell a compelling story.
   -  Share real world examples, including failures.
   -  Provide hard evidence, not platitudes.
   -  Deliver practical lessons people can use.

Attendees deserve more than panels. Heck, the entire cybersecurity industry deserves more than panels. So, join me in the “No More Panels” movement. You won’t regret it.
